{{Short description|Type of topological space}}
In [[topology]], a '''topological manifold''' is a [[topological space]] that locally resembles [[real numbers|real]] ''n''-[[dimension (mathematics)|dimensional]] [[Euclidean space]]. Topological manifolds are an important class of topological spaces, with applications throughout mathematics. All [[manifold]]s are topological manifolds by definition, so the qualifier "topological" emphasizes the lack of additional structure. E.g. [[differentiable manifold]]s are topological manifolds equipped with a [[differential structure]]. Every manifold has an "underlying" topological manifold, obtained by simply "forgetting" the added structure.<ref name="Bhatia2011">{{cite book|author=Rajendra Bhatia|title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians: Hyderabad, August 19-27, 2010|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GFE1vx2pynMC&pg=PA477|date=6 June 2011|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-981-4324-35-9|pages=477–}}</ref> However, not every topological manifold can be endowed with a particular additional structure. For example, the [[E8 manifold]] is a topological manifold which cannot be endowed with a differentiable structure.

== Formal definition ==

A [[topological space]] ''X'' is called '''locally Euclidean''' if there is a non-negative [[integer]] ''n'' such that every point in ''X'' has a [[neighborhood (topology)|neighborhood]] which is [[homeomorphic]] to an [[open set|open subset]] of [[real coordinate space|real ''n''-space]] '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>.<ref name="Lee2006">{{cite book|author=John M. Lee|title=Introduction to Topological Manifolds|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AdIRBwAAQBAJ|date=6 April 2006|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-0-387-22727-6}}</ref>

A '''topological manifold''' is a locally Euclidean [[Hausdorff space]]. It is common to place additional requirements on topological manifolds. In particular, many authors define them to be [[paracompact]]<ref name="Aubin2001">{{cite book|author=Thierry Aubin|title=A Course in Differential Geometry|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q2iS-aSeHK0C&pg=PA25|year=2001|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-7214-7|pages=25–}}</ref> or [[second-countable]].<ref name=" Lee2006 " />

In the remainder of this article a ''manifold'' will mean a topological manifold. An ''n-manifold'' will mean a topological manifold such that every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>.

== Examples ==
{{Main|List of manifolds}}

===''n''-manifolds===

* The [[real coordinate space]] '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> is an ''n''-manifold.
* Any [[discrete space]] is a 0-dimensional manifold.
* A [[circle]] is a [[compact space|compact]] 1-manifold.
* A [[torus]] and a [[Klein bottle]] are compact 2-manifolds (or [[Surface (topology)|surface]]s).
* The [[n-sphere|''n''-dimensional sphere]] ''S''<sup>''n''</sup> is a compact ''n''-manifold.
* The [[n-torus|''n''-dimensional torus]] '''T'''<sup>''n''</sup> (the product of ''n'' circles) is a compact ''n''-manifold.

===Projective manifolds===

* [[Projective space]]s over the [[real number|reals]], [[complex number|complexes]], or [[quaternion]]s are compact manifolds.
** [[Real projective space]] '''RP'''<sup>''n''</sup> is a ''n''-dimensional manifold.
** [[Complex projective space]] '''CP'''<sup>''n''</sup> is a 2''n''-dimensional manifold.
** [[Quaternionic projective space]] '''HP'''<sup>''n''</sup> is a 4''n''-dimensional manifold.
* Manifolds related to projective space include [[Grassmannian]]s, [[flag manifold]]s, and [[Stiefel manifold]]s.

===Other manifolds===

* [[Differentiable manifold]]s are a class of topological manifolds equipped with a [[differential structure]].
* [[Lens space]]s are a class of differentiable manifolds that are [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient]]s of odd-dimensional spheres.
* [[Lie group]]s are a class of differentiable manifolds equipped with a compatible [[Group (mathematics)|group]] structure.
* The [[E8 manifold]] is a topological manifold which cannot be given a differentiable structure.

== Properties ==

The property of being locally Euclidean is preserved by [[local homeomorphism]]s. That is, if ''X'' is locally Euclidean of dimension ''n'' and ''f'' : ''Y'' → ''X'' is a local homeomorphism, then ''Y'' is locally Euclidean of dimension ''n''. In particular, being locally Euclidean is a [[topological property]].

Manifolds inherit many of the local properties of Euclidean space. In particular, they are [[locally compact space|locally compact]], [[locally connected space|locally connected]], [[first-countable space|first countable]], [[locally contractible space|locally contractible]], and [[locally metrizable space|locally metrizable]]. Being locally compact Hausdorff spaces, manifolds are necessarily [[Tychonoff space]]s.

Adding the Hausdorff condition can make several properties become equivalent for a manifold. As an example, we can show that for a Hausdorff manifold, the notions of [[σ-compact]]ness and second-countability are the same. Indeed, a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff manifold]] is a locally compact Hausdorff space, hence it is (completely) regular.<ref>Topospaces subwiki, [http://topospaces.subwiki.org/wiki/Locally_compact_Hausdorff_implies_completely_regular Locally compact Hausdorff implies completely regular]</ref> Assume such a space X is σ-compact. Then it is Lindelöf, and because Lindelöf + regular implies paracompact, X is metrizable. But in a metrizable space, second-countability coincides with being Lindelöf, so X is second-countable. Conversely, if X is a Hausdorff second-countable manifold, it must be σ-compact.<ref>Stack Exchange, [https://math.stackexchange.com/q/57348 Hausdorff locally compact and second countable is sigma-compact]</ref>

A manifold need not be connected, but every manifold ''M'' is a [[disjoint union (topology)|disjoint union]] of connected manifolds. These are just the [[connected component (topology)|connected component]]s of ''M'', which are [[open set]]s since manifolds are locally-connected. Being locally path connected, a manifold is path-connected [[if and only if]] it is connected. It follows that the path-components are the same as the components.

===The Hausdorff axiom===

The Hausdorff property is not a local one; so even though Euclidean space is Hausdorff, a locally Euclidean space need [[Non-Hausdorff manifold| not be]]. It is true, however, that every locally Euclidean space is [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub>]].

An example of a non-Hausdorff locally Euclidean space is the [[line with two origins]]. This space is created by replacing the origin of the real line with ''two'' points, an open neighborhood of either of which includes all nonzero numbers in some open interval centered at zero. This space is not Hausdorff because the two origins cannot be separated.

===Compactness and countability axioms===

A manifold is [[metrizable space|metrizable]] if and only if it is [[paracompact]]. The [[Long line (topology)|long line]] is an example a [[Normal space|normal]] [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] 1-dimensional topological manifold that is not metrizable nor paracompact.  Since metrizability is such a desirable property for a topological space, it is common to add paracompactness to the definition of a manifold. In any case, non-paracompact manifolds are generally regarded as [[pathological (mathematics)|pathological]].  Paracompact manifolds have all the topological properties of metric spaces. In particular, they are [[perfectly normal Hausdorff space]]s.

Manifolds are also commonly required to be [[second-countable space|second-countable]]. This is precisely the condition required to ensure that the manifold [[embedding|embeds]] in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space. For any manifold the properties of being second-countable, [[Lindelöf space|Lindelöf]], and [[σ-compact space|σ-compact]] are all equivalent.

Every second-countable manifold is paracompact, but not vice versa. However, the converse is nearly true: a paracompact manifold is second-countable if and only if it has a [[countable set|countable]] number of [[connected component (topology)|connected component]]s. In particular, a connected manifold is paracompact if and only if it is second-countable. 
Every second-countable manifold is [[separable space|separable]] and paracompact. Moreover, if a manifold is separable and paracompact then it is also second-countable.

Every [[compact space|compact]] manifold is second-countable and paracompact.

===Dimensionality===

By [[invariance of domain]], a non-empty ''n''-manifold cannot be an ''m''-manifold for ''n'' ≠ ''m''.<ref name="Dieck2008">{{cite book|author=Tammo tom Dieck|title=Algebraic Topology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ruSqmB7LWOcC&pg=PA249|year=2008|publisher=European Mathematical Society|isbn=978-3-03719-048-7|pages=249–}}</ref> The dimension of a non-empty ''n''-manifold is ''n''. Being an ''n''-manifold is a [[topological property]], meaning that any topological space homeomorphic to an ''n''-manifold is also an ''n''-manifold.<ref name="Lee2010" />

==Coordinate charts==

By definition, every point of a locally Euclidean space has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of <math>\mathbb R^n </math>. Such neighborhoods are called ''Euclidean neighborhoods''. It follows from [[invariance of domain]] that Euclidean neighborhoods are always open sets. One can always find Euclidean neighborhoods that are homeomorphic to "nice" open sets in <math>\mathbb R^n </math>. Indeed, a space ''M'' is locally Euclidean if and only if either of the following equivalent conditions holds:
*every point of ''M'' has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an [[open ball]] in <math>\mathbb R^n </math>.
*every point of ''M'' has a neighborhood homeomorphic to <math>\mathbb R^n </math> itself.
A Euclidean neighborhood homeomorphic to an open ball in <math>\mathbb R^n </math> is called a ''Euclidean ball''. Euclidean balls form a [[basis (topology)|basis]] for the topology of a locally Euclidean space.

For any Euclidean neighborhood ''U'', a homeomorphism <math>\phi : U \rightarrow \phi \left ( U \right ) \subset \mathbb R^n </math>  is called a '''coordinate chart''' on ''U'' (although the word ''chart'' is frequently used to refer to the domain or range of such a map). A space ''M'' is locally Euclidean if and only if it can be [[cover (topology)|covered]] by Euclidean neighborhoods. A set of Euclidean neighborhoods that cover ''M'', together with their coordinate charts, is called an [[atlas (topology)|atlas]] on ''M''. (The terminology comes from an analogy with [[cartography]] whereby a spherical [[globe]] can be described by an [[atlas]] of flat maps or charts).

Given two charts <math>\phi</math> and <math>\psi</math> with overlapping domains ''U'' and ''V'', there is a ''transition function''
:<math>\psi\phi^{-1} : \phi \left ( U \cap V \right ) \rightarrow \psi \left ( U \cap V \right )</math>
Such a map is a homeomorphism between open subsets of <math>\mathbb R^n </math>. That is, coordinate charts agree on overlaps up to homeomorphism. Different types of manifolds can be defined by placing restrictions on types of transition maps allowed. For example, for [[differentiable manifolds]] the transition maps are required to be [[Diffeomorphism |smooth]].

==Classification of manifolds==

===Discrete spaces (0-Manifold)===
{{Main|Discrete space}}

A 0-manifold is just a [[discrete space]]. A discrete space is second-countable if and only if it is [[countable set|countable]].<ref name="Lee2010" />

===Curves (1-Manifold)===
{{Main|1-manifold}}

Every nonempty, paracompact, connected 1-manifold is homeomorphic either to '''R''' or the [[circle]].<ref name="Lee2010" />

===Surfaces (2-Manifold)===
{{Main|2-manifold|Classification theorem for surfaces}}
[[Image:Sphere wireframe.svg|thumb|The [[sphere]] is a 2-manifold.]]

Every nonempty, compact, connected 2-manifold (or [[Surface (topology)|surface]]) is homeomorphic to the [[sphere]], a [[connected sum]] of [[torus|tori]], or a connected sum of [[real projective plane|projective plane]]s.<ref name="GallierXu2013">{{cite book|author1=Jean Gallier|author2=Dianna Xu|title=A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces|title-link=A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces|date=5 February 2013|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-642-34364-3}}</ref>

===Volumes (3-Manifold)===
{{Main|3-manifold}}

A classification of 3-manifolds results from
[[Thurston's geometrization conjecture]], proven by [[Grigori Perelman]] in 2003. More specifically, Perelman's results provide an algorithm for deciding if two three-manifolds are homeomorphic to each other.<ref>{{cite book|title=Geometrisation of 3-manifolds|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uZqRpkLwS70C|year=2010|publisher=European Mathematical Society|isbn=978-3-03719-082-1}}</ref>

===General ''n''-manifold===
{{Main|4-manifold|5-manifold}}

The full classification of ''n''-manifolds for ''n'' greater than three is known to be impossible; it is at least as hard as the [[word problem for groups|word problem]] in [[group theory]], which is known to be [[undecidable problem|algorithmically undecidable]].<ref name="Conlon2013">{{cite book|author=Lawrence Conlon|title=Differentiable Manifolds: A First Course|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sj7rBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA90|date=17 April 2013|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4757-2284-0|pages=90–}}</ref>

In fact, there is no [[algorithm]] for deciding whether a given manifold is [[simply connected]]. There is, however, a classification of simply connected manifolds of dimension ≥ 5.<ref>Žubr A.V. (1988) Classification of simply-connected topological 6-manifolds. In: Viro O.Y., Vershik A.M. (eds) Topology and Geometry — Rohlin Seminar. Lecture Notes in Mathematics, vol 1346. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg</ref><ref>Barden, D. "Simply Connected Five-Manifolds." Annals of Mathematics, vol. 82, no. 3, 1965, pp. 365–385. JSTOR, www.jstor.org/stable/1970702.</ref>

===Manifolds with boundary===
{{Main|Manifold#Manifold with boundary}}

A slightly more general concept is sometimes useful. A '''topological manifold with boundary''' is a [[Hausdorff space]] in which every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of Euclidean [[Half-space (geometry)|half-space]] (for a fixed ''n''):
:<math>\mathbb R^n_{+} = \{(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \in \mathbb R^n : x_n \ge 0\}.</math>

Every topological manifold is a topological manifold with boundary, but not vice versa.<ref name="Lee2010" />

==Constructions==
There are several methods of creating manifolds from other manifolds.

===Product manifolds===

If ''M'' is an ''m''-manifold and ''N'' is an ''n''-manifold, the [[Cartesian product]] ''M''&times;''N'' is a (''m''+''n'')-manifold when given the [[product topology]].<ref name="LeeLee2009">{{cite book|author1=Jeffrey Lee|author2=Jeffrey Marc Lee|title=Manifolds and Differential Geometry|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QqHdHy9WsEoC&pg=PA7|year=2009|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-4815-9|pages=7–}}</ref>

===Disjoint union===

The [[disjoint union (topology)|disjoint union]] of a countable family of ''n''-manifolds is a ''n''-manifold (the pieces must all have the same dimension).<ref name="Lee2010">{{cite book|author=John Lee|title=Introduction to Topological Manifolds|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZQVGAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA64|date=25 December 2010|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4419-7940-7|pages=64–}}</ref>

===Connected sum===
{{Main|Connected sum}}

The [[connected sum]] of two ''n''-manifolds is defined by removing an open ball from each manifold and taking the [[quotient topology|quotient]] of the disjoint union of the resulting manifolds with boundary, with the quotient taken with regards to a homeomorphism between the boundary spheres of the removed balls. This results in another ''n''-manifold.<ref name="Lee2010" />

===Submanifold===
{{Main|Submanifold}}

Any open subset of an ''n''-manifold is an ''n''-manifold with the [[subspace topology]].<ref name="LeeLee2009" />
